--- title: "Monte-Carlo Sampling Distributions of the Residual-Field Mean" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 bibliography: references.bib --- ```{=html} ``` This report is **descriptive only**. It measures the sampling distribution of the residual-field domain mean under two designs — sampling that is uniform with respect to the analysis measure, and sampling by advected virtual floats — and displays those distributions. It constructs no test statistic and reports no $p$-value. Standard errors are given so the reader can judge what the Monte Carlo does and does not resolve. It is organized so that the assumptions enter in one place and as late as possible. 1. **The bias and its distribution**, from the aligned cells alone — the array advected by the same calendar year's flow as the field it samples. This is a direct Monte Carlo summary of realized designs and rests on no assumption whatever. It answers what the bias of an advectively sampled OHC estimate *is*, and stops there. 2. **Separating coverage bias from preferential sampling.** An advected array is non-representative for reasons unrelated to the field — retention, shelf thinning, a finite footprint — and would be biased against a field it was statistically independent of. Pairing each field year against nine *unaligned* flow years cancels that generic component exactly, by a zero-sum contrast along the flow-year axis, leaving the part attributable to flow and field sharing an ocean state. The cancellation is exact; recovering preferential sampling from what remains costs exactly one assumption, stated and probed there. The hypothesis test of `theory.tex` is built on these ensembles in a companion report, [A Permutation Test for Preferential Sampling](permutation_test.html), which states the assumptions it needs, tests the ones that are testable, and finds two of the four rejected by the data. Everything is run over **two analysis regions**: Box B, in the North Atlantic Current, and Box A, in the subtropical gyre. They are set up identically and reported side by side throughout, in panel-tabsets on every figure and table, so the two can be compared under one construction. Because their fields differ $3.3\times$ in amplitude, every cross-box comparison is made on the standardized scale $B/\sigma_k$. # Data and models **Field.** GLORYS12V1 reanalysis on its native $1/12^\circ$ grid. OHC is the $0$–$2000$ m depth integral of potential temperature against constant $c_p\rho$ (`code/ohc.py`), evaluated daily over 2010–2019. Cells enter the analysis only where $\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m *and* the integral is defined at every level, which is $92.4\%$ of Box B by area ($26{,}785$ cells) and $99.8\%$ of Box A ($34{,}863$ cells) — Box B loses its shelf edge, Box A is essentially all deep ocean. **Mean field.** Per-cell OLS of monthly OHC on $\{1,\,t,\,t^2,\,\sin 2\pi t,\,\cos 2\pi t,\, \sin 4\pi t,\,\cos 4\pi t\}$, fitted to the 1995–2019 monthly record with regressors averaged over each month to match what a monthly mean is. All cells share one design matrix, so the fit is a single pseudo-inverse. The residual field is $\tilde Z_k = \mathrm{OHC}_k - \hat m$, evaluated daily on the same mask. **Advection.** OceanParcels, park depth $1000$ m, driven by GLORYS daily $(u,v)$ over $15$–$50^\circ$ N, $70$–$30^\circ$ W. Floats advect continuously at park depth and record a position every $10$ days; there is no ascent, descent or surface drift, so a cycle is a position sample, not a simulated dive. Floats are deleted on leaving the velocity domain and retired at a lifespan drawn from the real Argo record for this region ($153$ deployments, median $1339$ d). **Estimation.** No model is fitted to the sampled values. $\hat Z$ is the unweighted mean of $\tilde Z_k$ at the profile positions, and $\bar Z_k$ is the exact $\mathbb{P}$-weighted domain mean of the same field; the comparison is arithmetic throughout. # The analysis domain Two analysis boxes sit inside the downloaded GLORYS region, both spanning $60^\circ$–$40^\circ$ W: **Box B** ($35$–$45^\circ$ N) straddles the North Atlantic Current and the Gulf Stream extension, and **Box A** ($22$–$34^\circ$ N) sits in the quiescent subtropical gyre. Temperature is downloaded over a common halo, from which the OHC truth and the fitted mean field are built; velocity is downloaded over a much larger region, because floats seeded near a box advect well outside it and return, and a float that leaves the velocity domain is lost from the experiment rather than merely lost from the box. ::: {#cell-fig-domain .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Analysis boxes inside the two downloaded GLORYS regions. OHC is integrated to $2000$ m, so a cell enters the estimand only where the water column reaches that depth; $88.7\%$ of the ocean cells in the advection domain do. The cut is not evenly distributed. **Box B loses $7.2\%$ of its area to it**, and that loss is concentrated in one corner: $99\%$ of its excluded cells lie north of $42^\circ$ N and $81\%$ west of $50^\circ$ W, on the Grand Banks and the Newfoundland shelf and rise. **Box A loses $0.08\%$** — $29$ cells, all isolated ridge and seamount tops in its eastern half. OHC runs $60$–$90$ GJ/m$^2$ and is almost entirely captured by the smooth mean field; $\tilde Z$ is a few GJ/m$^2$ of mesoscale structure. On the Box B day shown, domain-mean OHC is $67.9$ GJ/m$^2$ against a mean field of $66.5$ and a residual of $+1.45$. The mean field varies on two time scales, neither daily: the harmonics move the Box B domain mean by $3.80$ GJ/m$^2$ within a year ($1.50$ in Box A), the trend by $2.59$ across 2010–2019 ($0.96$), and consecutive days by $0.03$. Everything mesoscale and day-to-day is therefore left in $\tilde Z$. Three properties of $\tilde Z$ matter downstream. It is **strongly structured in space** at every quantile — even the 5th-percentile day carries a coherent front — which is what makes float position matter. That structure is **almost all of its variability**: Box B's median daily spatial spread is $6.63$ GJ/m$^2$ against a total $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z) = 6.81$ that also includes variation of the domain mean across days and years. And the two boxes differ several-fold in amplitude — daily spread spans $5.4$–$8.7$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B against $1.4$–$2.7$ in Box A — so bias and Monte Carlo error both scale with $\sigma_k$, and the boxes are comparable only on a standardized $B/\sigma_k$ scale. # Estimand, truth, and estimator Let $\mathbb{P}$ be the normalized area $\times$ time probability measure on the Box B analysis domain: the base measure is surface measure restricted to the wet native GLORYS cells ($\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m, intersected with the data support), $A_j = e1t_j\,e2t_j$, tensored with counting measure on the $365$ days of the year and normalized. The target is the residual field's domain mean, $$\bar Z_k \;=\; \int_{\mathcal{X}} \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P},$$ for each analysis year $k \in \{2010,\dots,2019\}$, where $\tilde Z_k$ is the year-$k$ OHC 0–2000 m field with the fitted mean field removed. A design is a finite point set $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \subset \mathcal{X}$; its estimator and bias are $$\hat Z^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde Z_k\!\left(x_i^{(l,d)}\right), \qquad B^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \hat Z^{(l,d)}_k - \bar Z_k .$$ $\tilde Z_k$ is a simple function on the native $1/12^\circ \times$ daily grid, so evaluation at $x_i$ is the cell-day lookup of the cell *containing* $x_i$ — not an interpolation. This is mean-field misfit, not a property of the sampling, and it **cancels from $B$ by construction** — $B$ differences a sample mean against the domain mean of the same field, so any spatially uniform offset $\delta_k$ in $\tilde Z_k$ drops out identically. It is carried in @tbl-truth rather than assumed away. The dispersion columns are the $\sigma_k$ that any cross-box comparison of $B$ must be standardized by: $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k)$ runs $6.3$–$7.6$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B against $1.7$–$2.4$ in Box A, a factor of $3.3$. It also trends upward through the decade in Box B ($6.3$ in 2013 to $7.6$ in 2019) while Box A's is flat, so even within Box B the same raw bias means different things in different years. # The two ensembles Both use the same $7{,}500$ designs' worth of sample sizes, so they differ only in *where* the points sit. **Advective.** $307$ floats per replicate (Box A: $357$) seeded uniformly with respect to *surface area* — equal-area in latitude, uniform in longitude — over the analysis box widened by $8^\circ$ and clipped to the velocity domain, then advected through velocity year $l$. Only profiles falling inside the analysis box enter $\hat Z$. Ten velocity years $l \in \{2010,\dots,2019\}$, $750$ independent replicates each, each paired with all ten analysis years: $l = k$ is **aligned** (flow and field the same calendar year), all others **unaligned**. The Box A float count was chosen to match Box B's over-density relative to real Argo (@tbl-argo), so the two grids differ in flow and field, not in how heavily they are sampled. The seeding rectangle is **not masked to ocean**, and Box B's reaches the North American coast, so $3.4\%$ of its seeds land on dry cells ($0.1\%$ in Box A). Those floats have no velocity, stay where they are, and keep emitting a position sample every cycle — the stationary dots over land in @fig-deploy. This costs array size and nothing else. It does not distort the deployment law: seeds that fall on ocean are still exactly area-uniform over the ocean part of the rectangle, since discarding the dry ones is a restriction to a sub-region rather than a reweighting within it. And it does not touch $\hat Z$, which evaluates $\tilde Z_k$ only on the analysis mask and drops everything else — of the first $3$ million gathered Box B profiles, none are on land. The effect is a $\sim\!3\%$ reduction in Box B's effective array, already absorbed into every measured quantity here, all of which are counted from what actually reported inside the box rather than from the nominal float count. **Deployment runs from 540 days before the analysis year (Box A: 720), and the array is in equilibrium when the window opens.** A constant release rate cannot reach equilibrium here — the empirical lifespan median is $1339$ d in Box B and $1560$ d in Box A, so the stock is still climbing after $900$ d. The release density $f$ is instead solved as a smooth non-negative deconvolution against the measured in-box response $g(u) = \mathbb{P}(\text{in box at age } u)$, $$\min_{f \ge 0}\; \lVert f * g - 1 \rVert^2 \;+\; \lambda \lVert D^2 f \rVert^2 ,$$ which front-loads $80\%$ of releases into the spin-up so the in-box stock is flat across $[0,360)$ rather than ramping. The roughness penalty is load-bearing: the unpenalized solution is a sparse vertex of the feasible set, and releasing in bursts would rebuild the cohort structure in float age that this design exists to remove. Box A needs the longer spin because its floats leave the box far more slowly — $g(1080) = 0.14$ there, so the deconvolution has a longer memory to fill — and $720$ d is the longest spin the $2010$–$2019$ velocity archive supports for a $2010$ analysis year. @tbl-stock shows the schedule in action. **Uniform (U-full).** For each advective design, $n$ iid draws with cell $\propto A_j$ and $\mathrm{doy} \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{0,\dots,364\}$ — a genuine iid sample from $\mathbb{P}$, matched to that design's own $n$. An advected array is non-representative for reasons that have nothing to do with $\tilde Z$ — it is retained in gyre interiors, thins over the shelf, and never samples some parts of the box at all — and such an array is biased against any field it is pointed at, including one it is statistically independent of. Separating that from sampling that responds to the field is the subject of the next section, and it costs an assumption. # Separating coverage bias from preferential sampling ## The identity the separation rests on For a fixed design $X = \{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ with empirical measure $\hat{\mathbb{P}}_X = n^{-1}\sum_i \delta_{x_i}$, the bias is *exactly* a bilinear pairing between the design and the field, $$B_k(X) \;=\; \int_{\mathcal{X}} \tilde Z_k \, d\big(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_X - \mathbb{P}\big) \;=\; \big\langle \mu_X, \, \tilde Z_k \big\rangle, \qquad \mu_X := \hat{\mathbb{P}}_X - \mathbb{P},$$ where $\mu_X$ is a signed measure of total mass zero on $\mathcal{X}$. No approximation enters: $\tilde Z_k$ is a bounded simple function and $\mu_X$ a finite signed measure, so the pairing is a well-defined Lebesgue integral and the identity is definitional. Decompose the design deviation into a part common to all flow years, a flow-year effect, and deployment noise, $$\mu^{(l,d)} \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; \delta^{(l)} \;+\; \eta^{(l,d)}, \qquad \bar\mu := \mathbb{E}_{l,d}\big[\mu^{(l,d)}\big], \qquad \delta^{(l)} := \mathbb{E}_d\big[\mu^{(l,d)}\big] - \bar\mu,$$ each again a zero-mass signed measure, with $\mathbb{E}_l[\delta^{(l)}] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}_d[\eta^{(l,d)}] = 0$ by construction. Pairing against $\tilde Z_k$ and using linearity, $$B^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \underbrace{\big\langle \bar\mu, \tilde Z_k \big\rangle}_{\text{coverage bias}} \;+\; \underbrace{\big\langle \delta^{(l)}, \tilde Z_k \big\rangle}_{\text{flow} \,\times\, \text{field}} \;+\; \big\langle \eta^{(l,d)}, \tilde Z_k \big\rangle .$$ **The first term is coverage bias**: the array's climatological footprint — where an advected array sits and when it reports, averaged over flow years — paired against field year $k$. It depends on $k$, because $\tilde Z_k$ changes; it does **not** depend on $l$. That is not an assumption but a property of the simulation: $X^{(l,d)}$ is generated from velocity year $l$ and the deployment law alone and never sees any analysis field, so $\bar\mu$ is a single fixed signed measure, free of $k$ by construction. It is exactly what @fig-heat shows as column structure, and exactly what the previous section's diagonal cannot exclude. Now form the contrast used throughout: $+1$ on the aligned flow and $-1/|\mathcal{C}_k|$ on each member of a comparison set $\mathcal{C}_k = \{l : |l-k| \ge 2\}$, which are weights summing to zero along $l$. The coverage term is constant in $l$, so it **cancels identically**: $$T_k \;=\; \bar B^{(k)}_k - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_k|}\sum_{l \in \mathcal{C}_k} \bar B^{(l)}_k \;=\; \big\langle \delta^{(k)}, \tilde Z_k \big\rangle \;-\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_k|}\sum_{l \in \mathcal{C}_k} \big\langle \delta^{(l)}, \tilde Z_k \big\rangle \;+\; O_p\!\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{MC}}\big),$$ the remainder being the deployment noise, which averages to zero and whose scale is quantified below. Cancellation of the coverage term is exact and assumption-free; it is the reason the unaligned cells are computed at all. ## The identifying assumption What survives is a difference of pairings between flow-year effects and the field. For $T_k$ to estimate preferential sampling, one assumption is required: > **(P)** For $l \in \mathcal{C}_k$, $\;\mathbb{E}\big[\langle \delta^{(l)}, \tilde Z_k\rangle\big] = 0$: > a *different* year's flow anomaly carries no information about year $k$'s field. Under (P) the unaligned cells estimate the same functional evaluated under independence of design and field, so their average is the null level of $\langle \delta^{(\cdot)}, \tilde Z_k \rangle$, and $T_k$ isolates the aligned pairing $\langle \delta^{(k)}, \tilde Z_k\rangle$ — a covariance between the design anomaly and the field, arising because in the aligned cell both are generated by the same ocean state. That is precisely $[S,X] \neq [S][X]$ in the sense of @diggle2010, restricted to the flow-anomaly component of the design. (P) is *not* implied by the simulation and is the one place this section is exposed. The threat is ocean memory: gyre state and the North Atlantic Oscillation persist over several years, so $\delta^{(l)}$ at small $|l-k|$ may retain dependence on $\tilde Z_k$. Contamination of that kind carries the sign of the aligned pairing and so **attenuates** $T_k$ toward zero, making it a conservative estimate rather than an unbiased one. The $|l-k| \ge 2$ gap in $\mathcal{C}_k$ is a guard against it, and @tbl-lag measures whether the guard is needed. Note what (P) does *not* require. It says nothing about the design being invariant across velocity years, nothing about exchangeability of flow years, and nothing about the distribution of $B$ — all of which are stronger conditions needed to convert $T_k$ into a $p$-value, and all of which fail here (see the companion report). The thinned designs are **nested** inside the full ones, so the two ensembles are correlated; this is the right construction for asking "does the same experiment survive at lower density", but it is not an independent replicate, and a genuinely independent Argo-density ensemble would cost a fresh simulation. And Box B is density-matched **on the mean of per-year ratios** ($0.99$), not on the ratio of pooled means ($0.82$): real Box B stock triples across the decade ($8.1$ in 2011 to $31.0$ in 2017) while the simulated array is constant by construction, so the thinned array is over-dense before 2015 and under-dense after. Box A has no such trend and matches on both ($1.00$ and $0.98$). # Caveats - **Two boxes are not a design.** Box B and Box A differ in field structure, current speed, retention, latitude and coastline at once. The cross-box comparison of @tbl-contrast is a two-point contrast between two named regions, not a controlled manipulation of any one of those, and nothing here identifies which of them the diagonal displacement depends on. A gradient-varying sweep of boxes, or the same box under rescaled velocities, would be needed for that. - **One flow realization per year.** The $750$ replicates per cell are independent *deployments*; the velocity field is a single realization of that calendar year. Every standard error quoted is over deployment randomness only, which is exactly why the between-flow scale, not the Monte Carlo se, is the right yardstick for the diagonal. - **No inference is drawn.** The aligned-minus-column contrast is reported as a measurement. Turning Box B's ten negative signs into a $p$-value — or Box A's mixed signs into a statement of no effect — needs an exchangeability assumption over velocity years given the field, which this design cannot test; that is deferred. In particular, Box A's null result is an absence of a measured displacement at this resolution ($0.0015$–$0.0020\,\sigma_k$ per cell), not a demonstration that no displacement exists. - **Assumption (P) is the one thing the separation cannot verify.** The cancellation of coverage bias is exact and follows from how the designs are generated, but reading what remains as preferential sampling needs $\mathbb{E}[\langle\delta^{(l)},\tilde Z_k\rangle] = 0$ for unaligned $l$. @tbl-lag finds no lag structure that would indicate a violation, which is evidence against contamination but not a proof of independence; multi-year ocean memory that is flat in $|l-k|$ over the observed range would be invisible to that check. Any such contamination carries the sign of the aligned pairing, so $T_k$ is attenuated rather than inflated by it. - **The between-flow scale is estimated from nine numbers.** Each box's implied between-flow sd comes from the spread of nine unaligned cells net of their own Monte Carlo error, so it is itself noisy, and it degenerates when the two are comparable — as in Box A's 2018, where the netting leaves $0.0005$ GJ/m$^2$ and the resulting ratio is meaningless. - **$n$ is endogenous.** Retention inside the box is an outcome of the flow, so $\hat Z$ is a ratio estimator, the sample sizes differ systematically by velocity year (@fig-nsize), and the two ensembles are matched conditional on $n$. Design-weighted and profile-weighted averages of the temporal component differ because $n$ and day-of-year coverage are correlated; the design-weighted average is the one consistent with $\mathbb{E}[B]$ and is used throughout. This bites harder in Box A, where retention is stronger and the design effect correspondingly larger (@tbl-deff-a). - **The main arms are denser than real Argo, and constant where the real one grows.** The simulated standing stock is $2.6\times$ the real Box B stock on average and up to $5.2\times$ in the sparse early years, and it is held fixed at $41$–$44$ floats while the real stock swings by a factor of $3.8$ across the decade (@tbl-argo). This leaves $\mathbb{E}[B]$ alone — the bias of a sample mean under a given deployment law does not depend on how many floats realize it — but the per-design spreads shown outside @tbl-density are roughly $\sqrt{2.6}\approx 1.6$ times narrower than a real array in this box would produce, so read those widths as a lower bound on real sampling variability. @tbl-density resolves the substantive half of this by rerunning the estimator at real density; what it cannot fix is the *constancy*, since a design tracking the real deployment history would confound array growth with the flow-year contrast. Box A carries the same mismatch at $2.4\times$, which is close enough to Box B's $2.6\times$ that the two boxes' widths remain comparable to each other even though neither is comparable to a real array. - **The seeding rectangle is not masked to ocean — known, deferred, to be fixed.** $3.4\%$ of Box B's seeds land on dry cells and are inert for the whole run ($0.1\%$ in Box A). Nothing here is wrong because of it: the surviving seeds stay exactly area-uniform over the ocean part of the rectangle, $\hat Z$ evaluates only on the analysis mask, and every count in this report is taken from what reported in-box rather than from the nominal float count. What it costs is $\sim\!3\%$ of Box B's effective array and a small asymmetry against Box A, which currently rides along inside the measured density ratios rather than being controlled. The fix is to reject seeds off the ocean mask at draw time in `deployment_plan_steady`; it changes the deployment law, so it needs a full re-simulation ($\approx 94$ CPU-h) and should be batched with any other change that also requires one — a genuinely independent Argo-density ensemble being the obvious candidate. - **Profiling is synchronized across floats.** Trajectory output is written on a fixed cadence from the run start, so all virtual floats profile on the same $36$ days of the year rather than each cycling from its own deployment date, as real Argo floats do (@tbl-stock). The realized day-of-year marginal is therefore supported on $36$ atoms rather than spread over the year, which is part of why the temporal component varies so little across designs. It does not bias $\hat Z$ on its own — the epochs are near-uniformly spaced — but it understates the temporal diversity a real array would have, and any statement here about day-of-year coverage should be read with that in mind. - **The spin-up ages the array.** Holding the standing stock flat requires releasing $\sim\!80\%$ of floats before the analysis year, which leaves the in-box age distribution older than a constant-rate array would give. The alternative — accepting the ramp — puts a far larger artefact into the day-of-year marginal, so this is the lesser distortion, but it is a distortion. - **$\tilde Z$ inherits the mean-field fit.** The seasonal residual driving the temporal term is itself what the trend-plus-harmonics basis failed to absorb; a different mean-field specification would move it. @tbl-truth reports the fit's leftover offset per year, which is largest in 2010–2014. # Appendix: every standard deviation and standard error, derived This appendix is self-contained. It defines each dispersion measure the report and its companion quote, derives the relation each one is claimed to satisfy, and closes with a numerical check that every relation holds on the actual ensembles. Read it as the audit trail for the uncertainty statements made above. ## A.1 What is random Three independent sources of randomness are in play, and almost every mistake in this area comes from conflating them. Fix an analysis year $k$ throughout. | symbol | source | replication available | |---|---|---| | $x_i$ | where a given design's profiles fall | $n$ per design | | $\omega$ | the deployment draw: seeds, release days, lifespans | $D = 750$ per velocity year | | $l$ | which calendar year's velocity field advects them | $M = 10$, **one realization each** | The residual fields $\{\tilde Z_k\}$ are **not** random: every quantity below is conditional on the realized GLORYS decade. The estimand $\bar Z_k = \int \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P}$ is therefore a fixed number, not a parameter with a sampling distribution. ## A.2 Dispersion of the field, $\sigma_k$ With $\mathbb{P}$ the normalized area $\times$ time measure on the wet analysis cells, $$\sigma_k^2 \;=\; \int \tilde Z_k^2 \, d\mathbb{P} \;-\; \Big(\int \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P}\Big)^2 .$$ Writing $\mathbb{P} = \mathbb{P}_{\text{space}} \otimes \mathrm{Unif}\{1,\dots,365\}$ and conditioning on the day gives an exact variance decomposition, $$\sigma_k^2 \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_d\big[\mathrm{Var}_{\text{space}}(\tilde Z_k(\cdot, d))\big]}_{\text{within-day spatial structure}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_d\big(\bar Z_k(d)\big)}_{\text{day-to-day movement of the domain mean}} .$$ The first term is what @fig-days displays and is $96.5$–$99.6\%$ of the total; the second is what makes day-of-year coverage able to bias $\hat Z$ at all, and is the $\bar Z_k(d)$ dispersion quoted in the temporal/spatial section. Verified exactly (row 1 of @tbl-audit). ## A.3 One design: the sampling variance of $\hat Z$ **Uniform (U-full).** A design is $n$ iid draws from $\mathbb{P}$, so conditional on $n$, $\mathbb{E}[\hat Z \mid n] = \bar Z_k$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat Z \mid n) = \sigma_k^2 / n$. Since $\mathbb{E}[B \mid n] = 0$ for *every* $n$, the law of total variance leaves no between-$n$ term: $$\mathrm{Var}(B) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{Var}(B \mid n)\big] + \mathrm{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[B \mid n]\big) \;=\; \sigma_k^2 \, \mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{n}\right] .$$ This is the "iid prediction" column of @tbl-ref, and it is $\mathbb{E}[1/n]$ rather than $1/\mathbb{E}[n]$ — the difference is Jensen's, $1.4\%$ here, but it is the correct form. Verified to $1.4\%$ (row 3). **Advective.** Consecutive cycles of one float are near-replicates, so the profiles are clustered. The float-clustered design effect $$\mathrm{deff}_k \;=\; \frac{\sum_f \big(\sum_{i \in f} (\tilde Z_{k,i} - \hat Z_k)\big)^2}{\sum_i (\tilde Z_{k,i} - \hat Z_k)^2}$$ is the usual cluster-sampling ratio, estimating $1 + (\bar m - 1)\rho$ for mean cluster size $\bar m$ and intra-float correlation $\rho$. It gives an effective sample size $n_{\text{eff}} = n/\mathrm{deff}_k$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat Z) \approx \mathrm{deff}_k \, \sigma_k^2/n$, so at matched $n$ the advective ensemble should be $\sqrt{\mathrm{deff}_k}$ times wider than the uniform one. That is exactly the "ratio" column of @tbl-deff against the square root of the "median design effect" column, and it holds to $3.5\%$ (row 4). **The width gap between the two ensembles is dependence, not bias.** ## A.4 One cell: the two-level model A cell of the grid is a pair $(k, l)$ holding $D$ designs. Write $$B_k^{(l,d)} \;=\; \beta_k \;+\; a_{kl} \;+\; \varepsilon_{kld}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(a_{kl}) = \sigma_a^2, \quad \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_{kld}) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2,$$ with $a$ the **flow-year effect** — what velocity year $l$ does to the sampling weights — and $\varepsilon$ the **deployment noise** from §A.3, whose variance is $\sigma_k^2 \mathbb{E}[1/n]$ inflated by the design effect. The cell mean is $\bar G_{kl} = \beta_k + a_{kl} + \bar\varepsilon$. Two different standard deviations follow, and the whole argument of the report turns on keeping them apart: $$\underbrace{\mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{MC}} \;=\; \sigma_\varepsilon/\sqrt{D}}_{\text{flow held fixed}}, \qquad \underbrace{\mathrm{sd}(\bar G_{kl}) \;=\; \sqrt{\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/D}}_{\text{flow varying}} .$$ $\mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{MC}}$ is the "MC se" / "$\mathrm{se}_B$" column everywhere in this report. It answers *"could this deployment ensemble have landed here by deployment randomness, with the flow held at year $l$?"* — and only that. **Estimating $\sigma_a$.** Two routes, both method-of-moments and both used above: 1. *Netting* (@tbl-aligned): the spread $s^2$ of the nine unaligned cell means estimates $\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/D$, so $\hat\sigma_a^2 = \max(0,\, s^2 - \overline{\mathrm{se}}^2)$. 2. *One-way ANOVA on $\mathcal{C}_k$* (`tbl-d1` of the companion report): $\mathrm{MS}_w$ estimates $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ and $\mathrm{MS}_b$ estimates $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + D\sigma_a^2$, giving $\hat\sigma_a^2 = (\mathrm{MS}_b - \mathrm{MS}_w)/D$. They target the same quantity and agree to $4\%$ ($0.0244$ vs $0.0234$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B, $0.0060$ vs $0.0063$ in Box A); they differ only in which flows enter. Both can go negative and are clipped at zero, and both degenerate when $D\sigma_a^2 \lesssim \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ — Box A's 2018, where the netting leaves $0.0005$ GJ/m$^2$ and the resulting ratio is meaningless. ## A.5 Monte-Carlo error itself Every "se" in these reports is a **Monte-Carlo** error: the uncertainty in a quantity from having simulated finitely many replicates, not sampling uncertainty about a population. The generic result is one line. If $\hat\theta = R^{-1}\sum_{r} \theta_r$ averages $R$ iid replicates of a quantity with variance $\tau^2$, then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = \tau^2/R$ and the reported se is the plug-in $$\widehat{\mathrm{se}} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{R}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{R-1}\sum_r (\theta_r - \hat\theta)^2} .$$ What changes between the tables is only $R$ and what a "replicate" is: | se | replicate | $R$ | |---|---|---| | `se_B`, `MC se`, `aligned MC se` (per grid cell) | one deployment $\omega$, flow year fixed | $D = 750$ | | `MC se` (@tbl-ref, whole uniform ensemble) | one uniform design, flows pooled | $N = MD = 7500$ | | permutation $p$-value | one relabelling $\lambda$ | $N_{\mathrm{perm}} = 10{,}000$ | The per-cell se uses $D = 750$ because it is deliberately *conditional on the flow year* — pooling to $7500$ would mix in the between-flow variation the report is trying to isolate. The uniform-ensemble se legitimately uses all $7500$ because under U-full there is no flow-year effect to preserve: the designs are iid draws from $\mathbb{P}$ regardless of which advective design supplied their $n$. **The error on the error.** A plug-in se is itself estimated. For roughly Gaussian replicates its relative standard deviation is $1/\sqrt{2(R-1)}$: $2.6\%$ at $R = 750$, $0.8\%$ at $R = 7500$, $0.7\%$ at $R = 10{,}000$. So the per-cell standard errors quoted to three decimals are meaningful in their first two digits and no further. **Monte-Carlo error of a $p$-value.** A permutation $p$-value is a binomial proportion over $N_{\mathrm{perm}}$ relabellings, so $\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/N_{\mathrm{perm}}}$: $0.0008$ at $\hat p = 0.0068$ (Box A) and $0.004$ at $\hat p = 0.23$ (Box A thinned). The $+1$ in $(1 + \#\{\cdot\})/(1 + N_{\mathrm{perm}})$ is the Davison–Hinkley correction, which keeps the test exact by counting the observed labelling as one of its own null replicates; it also fixes the attainable minimum at $1/(1+N_{\mathrm{perm}}) = 10^{-4}$. A $p$-value *at* that floor should be read as "$< 10^{-4}$, unresolved", never as a point estimate. **Monte-Carlo error of the variance components.** This is the loosest link in the chain and deserves stating plainly. For a balanced one-way layout with $a$ groups of $D$, $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\sigma_a^2) \;=\; \frac{1}{D^2}\left[\frac{2\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MS}_b]^2}{a-1} \;+\; \frac{2\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MS}_w]^2}{a(D-1)}\right], \qquad \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MS}_b] = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + D\sigma_a^2 .$$ The first term dominates completely, and it is divided by $a - 1 \in \{6, 7\}$ — **the precision of $\hat\sigma_a$ is set by the number of flow years, not by the $750$ deployments inside each.** Evaluating at the measured components gives a relative standard deviation on $\hat\sigma_a$ of $31$–$41\%$ in Box B (median $34\%$) and $31$–$290\%$ in Box A, the upper end being the degenerate 2018 cell. The observed across-year scatter of $\hat\sigma_a$ — $26\%$ and $43\%$ — is consistent with that, the Box B value running lower because the ten analysis years share the same flows and so their estimates are correlated. This propagates. The inflation factor of §A.8 is roughly proportional to $\hat\sigma_a$ once $D\sigma_a^2 \gg \sigma_\varepsilon^2$, so a $34\%$ uncertainty on $\hat\sigma_a$ carries through nearly one-for-one. Read "inflation $1.6$–$3.9$" as a factor of roughly $2.5$ known to within about a third, not as six significant figures — which is enough to establish that the permutation null is materially too narrow, and not enough to correct it to a specific number. That is exactly why §A.8 is presented as a sensitivity and not as a repaired test. **What carries no Monte-Carlo error.** $\bar Z_k$, $\sigma_k$ and the daily spreads are exhaustive computations over the whole field, not simulations; the quantile-day selection in @fig-days is a lookup over all $3{,}650$ days; and the sign test is exact combinatorics. None of these have an se, and none is quoted with one. ## A.6 The contrast, and the $(1 + 1/|\mathcal{C}_k|)$ factor The aligned-minus-comparison contrast is $T_k = \bar G_{kk} - |\mathcal{C}_k|^{-1}\sum_{l \in \mathcal{C}_k} \bar G_{kl}$. If the cell means are independent with common variance $v$, then since the second term averages $c = |\mathcal{C}_k|$ of them, $$\mathrm{Var}(T_k) \;=\; v + \frac{v}{c} \;=\; v\Big(1 + \frac{1}{c}\Big), \qquad v \;=\; \sigma_a^2 + \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{D} .$$ With $c \in \{7, 8\}$ the factor is $1.14$–$1.13$, i.e. the contrast is only $\sim\!7\%$ noisier than a single cell mean. The report's earlier "aligned $-$ column mean" uses all ten velocity years including the aligned one, which changes the coefficients slightly and the numbers negligibly. ## A.7 Pooling across analysis years $\bar T = m^{-1}\sum_k T_k$ is reported with the **empirical across-year standard error** $\mathrm{sd}(\{T_k\})/\sqrt{m}$, not with a Monte-Carlo error propagated through §A.4. That choice is deliberate and its assumption should be stated plainly: **it is consistent only if the $T_k$ are independent across $k$**. They are not exactly, because all ten share the same $M$ velocity years, so their $a$-components are common rather than independent and $\mathrm{Cov}(T_k, T_{k'}) \neq 0$. The empirical version at least contains the flow variance, whereas the MC-propagated version excludes it entirely and would be far too small; neither is exact. This is the same limitation that blocks a valid pooled test, and it is why the report treats $\bar T$ descriptively. ## A.8 The permutation null, and why it is narrow Relabelling assigns the $N = MD$ designs at random to $M$ groups of $D$. Because $\sum_g \bar G_g$ is then a fixed constant, $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_g \bar G_g) = 0$ forces $\mathrm{Cov}(\bar G_g, \bar G_h) = -\mathrm{Var}(\bar G)/(M-1)$, while simple random sampling without replacement gives $\mathrm{Var}(\bar G_g) = (S^2/D)(1 - 1/M)\,N/(N-1)$ with $S^2$ the pooled variance of all $N$ design values. Substituting both into $\mathrm{Var}(T_k)$ and simplifying, the $M$-dependence cancels exactly: $$\mathrm{Var}_{\mathrm{perm}}(T_k) \;=\; \Big(1 + \frac{1}{c}\Big)\frac{S^2}{D}\cdot\frac{N}{N-1} .$$ Verified to $3\%$ (row 5). Now the crux. The pooled $S^2$ *mixes* flow years, so $S^2 \approx \sigma_a^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2$, whereas §A.6 gives the true variance as $(1 + 1/c)(\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/D)$. The ratio is $$\frac{\mathrm{sd}_{\text{true}}(T_k)}{\mathrm{sd}_{\mathrm{perm}}(T_k)} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{D\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}} ,$$ which is the inflation factor tabulated in the companion report, verified to $7\%$ (row 6). Two consequences worth stating explicitly: - The permutation null contains $\sigma_a^2/D$ where the truth has $\sigma_a^2$. It divides the flow-year variance by the number of *deployments*, which is not a replication of flows at all. - **More replicates make the test worse.** As $D \to \infty$ the permutation sd $\to 0$ like $D^{-1/2}$ while the true sd $\to \sqrt{(1+1/c)\,\sigma_a^2} > 0$. At $D = 750$ with Box B's components the factor is $2.6$; at $D = 7500$ it would be $7.8$. Nothing about increasing Monte-Carlo effort repairs it. ## A.9 Standardization The boxes differ $3.3\times$ in field amplitude, so cross-box comparison uses $B/\sigma_k$ and $T_k/\sigma_k$ throughout.
